answer.rationale: Temporal coincidence is the strongest signal available: the release landed 2h ago and p99 write latency has been climbing 90m, so the release is the leading candidate cause. Rollback is the only option that attacks a suspected cause rather than redistributing symptoms, and it is the least threatening to the 'no lost customer writes' constraint. Regional failover (memory_b2) is the seductive alternative because the degradation is region-confined, but b2's success was during a March infrastructure degradation, not a post-release regression; failing over at peak settlement write volume risks replication-lag write loss, which directly violates the primary objective, and it would carry a bad build into the secondary region. add_capacity (b3) was pre-provisioned headroom ahead of a known peak, not a mid-incident lever, and it does nothing if the cause is code. route_read_replicas (b5) treated read-driven contention from dashboards; nothing here indicates read pressure, and it would not touch a write-path regression. Circuit breakers (b4) contained an external partner outage; this degradation is internal and breaking the write path would shed exactly the writes we must preserve. I am verifying memory_b1 rather than the alternatives because b1 is the memory my chosen action leans on, and its archived record is where the load-bearing detail sits: whether the day-18 rollback was clean because the prior build was genuinely compatible, or because traffic was light and no schema/data migration had to be reversed. If day 18 was a low-write-volume window with no migration, its reassurance does not transfer to peak settlement, and rollback may itself be write-hostile. Explicit downstream risk: rollback is irreversible in effect if the new release included a forward-only schema or data migration, in which case reverting the build could corrupt or reject in-flight settlement writes; a rollback that fails also consumes the single intervention window and leaves us worse off at peak. Hence small_guarded_test scale: revert on a canary cohort of write traffic first, per the staged-gating pattern in b6, and watch p99 and write-success rate before widening. I hold real uncertainty: region-confinement is equally consistent with a primary-region infrastructure fault that has nothing to do with the release, and a canary rollback that does not move p99 is the signal that discriminates between those two worlds.
